# Polycythemia vera

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Hematology and oncology > Red blood cell disorders > Polycythemia vera*

[Original Article Link](/library/kT0mI2)

---

## Summary

Polycythemia vera is a chronic <u>myeloproliferative neoplasm</u> most commonly caused by a <u>gain of function mutation</u> in the <u>JAK2 gene</u>, leading to <u>erythrocytosis</u> with or without increases in <u>granulocytes</u> and <u>platelets</u>. The elevated blood cell mass results in hyperviscosity, which may manifest with fatigue, <u>facial flushing</u>, <u>pruritus</u>, <u>erythromelalgia</u>, <u>headaches</u>, <u>dizziness</u>, and, in severe cases, <u>thromboembolic events</u> (e.g., <u>stroke</u>, <u>Budd-Chiari syndrome</u>). Diagnosis is confirmed if other <u>causes of polycythemia</u> are ruled out (e.g., <u>relative polycythemia</u>, <u>hypoxia</u>-induced <u>polycythemia</u>, autonomous <u>EPO</u> production) and <u>diagnostic criteria for polycythemia vera</u> are met. Management of polycythemia vera focuses on preventing <u>thrombotic</u> and bleeding events and treating associated symptoms (e.g., <u>pruritus</u>, <u>gout</u>). <u>Therapeutic phlebotomy</u> and <u>aspirin</u> are indicated in all patients. Additionally, patients with <u>high-risk polycythemia vera</u> require <u>cytoreductive therapies</u> and, possibly, anticoagulation. Patients should be monitored carefully for the development of complications and transformation of polycythemia vera to another hematologic <u>malignancy</u>, e.g., <u>post-PV myelofibrosis</u>, myelodysplasia, or <u>acute myelogenous leukemia</u> (<u>AML</u>).




![Polycythemia vera fact sheet](media/xzfb5czdykmz2n2dqqizbu7k.jpg)

Polycythemia vera fact sheet

---

## Pathophysiology

* The <u>JAK2</u> (<u>Janus kinase 2</u>) <u>oncogene</u> codes for a <u>non-receptor tyrosine kinase</u> in <u>hematopoietic</u> progenitor cells. <u>JAK2</u> is essential for the regulation of <u>erythropoiesis</u>, <u>thrombopoiesis</u> (<u>megakaryopoiesis</u>), and <u>granulopoiesis</u>.

* 98% of patients with <u>polycythemia</u> vera have a mutation in the <u>JAK2 gene</u> (<u>gain of function</u>) → ↑ <u>tyrosine kinase</u> activity → <u>erythropoietin</u>-independent <u>proliferation</u> of the myeloid cell lines → ↑ blood cell mass (<u>erythrocytosis</u>, <u>thrombocytosis</u>, and <u>granulocytosis</u>) → hyperviscosity and slow blood flow → ↑ risk of <u>thrombosis</u> and poor oxygenation.

---

## Clinical features

* Often asymptomatic (incidental finding on routine blood tests)

* Nonspecific symptoms: fatigue, difficulty concentrating, <u>insomnia</u>, abdominal <u>pain</u>

* <u>Constitutional symptoms</u>: weight loss, sweating

* <u>Hyperviscosity syndrome</u>: triad of <u>mucosal</u> bleeding, neurological symptoms, and visual changes

* <u>Plethora</u>; : flushed face with a purple hue; <u>cyanotic</u> <u>lips</u>

* <u>Pruritus</u>; : Itching typically worsens when the <u>skin</u> comes into contact with warm water (<u>aquagenic pruritus</u>).

* <u>Erythromelalgia</u>  [[8]](/library/NUX-Wx)

* Nonspecific neurological symptoms : <u>dizziness</u>, <u>headache</u>, visual disturbances, <u>tinnitus</u>

* <u>Hypertension</u>

* <u>Splenomegaly</u> : associated with early satiety and abdominal discomfort; less commonly <u>hepatomegaly</u>

* <u>Peptic ulcer disease</u>

* <u>Gout</u>

* Symptoms of <u>thrombotic</u> and hemorrhagic complications (see “Complications” below)





> [!TIP]
> Patients with <u>polycythemia</u> vera are at increased risk of <u>thrombosis</u> and bleeding.

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[3]](/library/0P1eWS0)[[9]](/library/g01F220)[[10]](/library/YYYnnn)[[11]](/library/H_cKpU0)




* Suspect polycythemia vera in:

* Individuals with elevated <u>hemoglobin</u> and/or <u>hematocrit</u>;   and normal <u>oxygen saturation</u>

* Patients with features or <u>complications associated with polycythemia vera</u> (e.g., <u>hyperviscosity syndrome</u>, <u>splanchnic vein thrombosis</u>)

* Rule out other <u>causes of polycythemia</u> based on a thorough <u>medical history</u>, <u>physical examination</u>, and diagnostics as needed.

* Order confirmatory <u>laboratory studies</u> for polycythemia vera.

* Serum <u>erythropoietin</u> levels (<u>EPO</u>)

* Peripheral blood screen for <u>JAK2</u> mutation  [[3]](/library/0P1eWS0)[[12]](/library/MPcM2c0)

* Consider <u>bone marrow</u> studies in consultation with <u>hematology</u>.  > 18.5 g/dL> 16.5 g/dL [[9]](/library/g01F220)[[10]](/library/YYYnnn)

* Consider abdominal imaging to evaluate for <u>splenomegaly</u>.

* Confirm diagnosis based on the <u>diagnostic criteria for polycythemia vera</u>.

* Reevaluate for other <u>causes of polycythemia</u> vera if diagnostic criteria are not met.





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Erythrocytosis</u> associated with normal <u>oxygen saturation</u> and decreased serum <u>EPO</u> levels is strongly suggestive of polycythemia vera. <u>Erythrocytosis</u> associated with elevated serum <u>EPO</u> or decreased <u>oxygen saturation</u> suggests <u>secondary polycythemia</u> caused by chronic <u>hypoxia</u>.




> [!WARNING]
> The first presentation in patients with polycythemia vera may be a <u>thrombotic event</u>, in particular, <u>hepatic vein thrombosis</u>. Maintain a low threshold for working up older patients with new <u>thrombosis</u>. [[13]](/library/FVXgwC)




### Diagnostic criteria




| <br>Diagnostic criteria for polycythemia vera  [[9]](/library/g01F220)[[10]](/library/YYYnnn)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
|  | Findings |
| Major criteria | <br><br>* <u>Erythrocytosis</u> (increased <u>RBCs</u>) as evidenced by any of the following:<br><br>* ↑ <u>Hgb</u> (<u>♂</u>: > 16.5 g/dL; <u>♀</u>: > 16 g/dL) [[10]](/library/YYYnnn)<br><br>* ↑ HCT (<u>♂</u>: > 49%; <u>♀</u>: > 48%) [[10]](/library/YYYnnn)<br><br>* ↑ <u>Red cell mass</u> (≥ 25% greater than the mean normal predictive value)   [[10]](/library/YYYnnn)<br><br>* <u>JAK2</u> mutation  [[3]](/library/0P1eWS0)[[12]](/library/MPcM2c0)<br><br>* <u>Bone marrow</u> studies<br><br>* Trilinear <u>hematopoietic</u> <u>proliferation</u> (<u>erythropoiesis</u>, <u>granulopoiesis</u>, <u>megakaryopoiesis</u>)<br><br>* Hypercellularity<br><br>* <u>Pleomorphic</u> mature <u>megakaryocytes</u><br><br><br> |
| Minor criterion | <br>* ↓ <u>EPO</u><br><br> |
| <br>Diagnostic confirmation <br><br>* All three major criteria are present<br><br>* OR <u>JAK2</u> mutation is not detected but two major criteria PLUS minor criterion are met<br><br><br><br> |  |





> [!TIP]
> <u>Hemoglobin</u> levels may be normal in the prepolycythemic (masked) phase of polycythemia vera, elevated during the overt <u>polycythemic</u> phase, and then decreased in <u>post-PV myelofibrosis</u> (the spent phase). [[13]](/library/FVXgwC)[[14]](/library/6b1ju20)




> [!TIP]
> <u>Bone marrow biopsy</u> may not be routinely required in patients with extremely elevated <u>Hgb</u> and <u>Hct</u> (i.e., <u>♂</u>: <u>Hgb</u> > 18.5 g/dL, <u>Hct</u> 55.5%; <u>♀</u>: > 16.5 g/dL, <u>Hct</u> 49.5%). [[3]](/library/0P1eWS0)[[9]](/library/g01F220)[[10]](/library/YYYnnn)




![Polycythemia vera](media/jgiktdqitz2xsrclvzx8zavx.jpg)

Polycythemia vera




### Findings on routine <u>laboratory studies</u> [[3]](/library/0P1eWS0)




Confirmatory <u>laboratory studies</u> are detailed in “<u>Diagnostic criteria for polycythemia vera</u>.” Additional findings on routine <u>laboratory studies</u> for <u>polycythemia</u> include: [[10]](/library/YYYnnn)[[15]](/library/R01lf20)




* <u>CBC</u>

* Normal or ↑ <u>platelets</u>  [[13]](/library/FVXgwC)

* Normal or ↑ <u>leukocytes</u>  [[13]](/library/FVXgwC)

* <u>ESR</u>: ↓ or normal  [[16]](/library/i01Jf20)

* <u>Peripheral smear</u> [[13]](/library/FVXgwC)[[17]](/library/kIYm1q)

* <u>Normocytic</u> normochromic <u>RBCs</u>

* If <u>iron deficiency anemia</u> is present, <u>microcytic</u>, <u>hypochromic</u> <u>RBCs</u>

* Serum <u>iron studies</u>: ↓ <u>iron</u>, ↓ <u>ferritin</u>  [[18]](/library/7b14E20)

* Markers of cell turnover: ↑ <u>leukocyte alkaline phosphatase</u>, <u>uric acid</u>, and/or <u>LDH</u>  [[17]](/library/kIYm1q)





> [!TIP]
> Polycythemia vera may manifest with <u>erythrocytosis</u> alone or, in > 50% of patients, <u>erythrocytosis</u> in combination with <u>leukocytosis</u> and/or <u>thrombocytosis</u>. [[9]](/library/g01F220)




> [!TIP]
> In patients with polycythemia vera and <u>iron deficiency</u>, microscopic findings of <u>iron deficiency anemia</u> (i.e., <u>microcytic hypochromic anemia</u>) are seen on <u>peripheral blood smear</u>, but with elevated rather than decreased <u>hemoglobin</u> levels. [[13]](/library/FVXgwC)[[17]](/library/kIYm1q)




> [!TIP]
> <u>Microcytic</u> <u>erythrocytosis</u> is only associated with polycythemia vera, <u>beta-thalassemia</u> trait, and <u>hypoxic</u> <u>erythrocytosis</u>. [[13]](/library/FVXgwC)[[17]](/library/kIYm1q)

---

## Differential diagnoses

* Other <u>causes of polycythemia</u>: See below.

* Absolute erythrocytosis

* Caused by an increased production of <u>RBCs</u> (normal plasma volume)

* Includes <u>primary polycythemia</u> and <u>secondary polycythemia</u>

* <u>Relative erythrocytosis</u> is caused by a decrease in plasma volume (normal <u>RBC mass</u>).

* Other <u>myeloproliferative disorders</u>: See “<u>Overview of MPNs</u>.”





| <br>Causes of polycythemia [[17]](/library/kIYm1q) |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | Definition | Characteristic features | Underlying conditions |
| Primary polycythemia |  | <br>* <u>Polycythemia</u> caused by a <u>bone marrow</u> defect<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>RBC mass</u>: ↑<br><br>* <u>EPO</u>: typically ↓<br><br>* <u>Oxygen saturation</u> (<u>SaO<sub>2</sub></u>) : normal<br><br>* Expected plasma volume: normal<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Polycythemia vera<br><br>* <u>Primary familial and congenital polycythemia</u> [[19]](/library/Bb1zD20)<br><br><br> |
| Secondary polycythemia | Physiologically appropriate secondary polycythemia | <br>* <u>Polycythemia</u> due to the physiological response to cellular <u>hypoxia</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>RBC mass</u>: ↑<br><br>* <u>EPO</u>: ↑<br><br>* <u>SaO<sub>2</sub></u>: ↓ or normal<br><br>* Expected plasma volume: normal or ↓<br><br><br> | <br><br>* With decreased <u>oxygen saturation</u><br><br>* High-altitude exposure<br><br>* <u>Hypoxia</u>, e.g., chronic pulmonary and cardiac disease<br><br>* With normal <u>oxygen saturation</u><br><br>* Intermittent <u>hypoxia</u>: <u>obstructive sleep apnea</u> (<u>OSA</u>)<br><br>* Smoker's polycythemia<br><br>* Congenital causes, e.g.:<br><br>* <u>Methemoglobinemia</u><br><br>* <u>Hemoglobinopathies</u> with an increased <u>Hb-O<sub>2</sub></u> affinity<br><br><br> |
| Physiologically inappropriate secondary polycythemia | <br>* <u>Polycythemia</u> secondary to conditions associated with autonomous production of <u>erythropoietin</u>, renal diseases that affect the <u>erythropoietin</u>-secreting cells, and <u>neoplasms</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>RBC mass</u>: ↑<br><br>* <u>EPO</u>: ↑↑<br><br>* <u>SaO<sub>2</sub></u>: normal<br><br>* Expected plasma volume: normal<br><br><br> | <br>* Autonomous <u>EPO</u> production, e.g.: [[17]](/library/kIYm1q)<br><br>* <u>Liver</u>: <u>hepatocellular carcinoma</u> (<u>HCC</u>) or hepatoma<br><br>* <u>Kidney</u>: <u>renal cell carcinoma</u> (<u>RCC</u>), <u>renal cysts</u> (e.g., PKD), <u>renal artery stenosis</u><br><br>* <u>Uterine leiomyoma</u><br><br>* <u>Cerebellar</u> <u>hemangioma</u><br><br> |  |
| Medication-induced polycythemia | <br>* <u>Polycythemia</u> secondary to medications that stimulate <u>erythrocytosis</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>RBC mass</u>: ↑<br><br>* <u>EPO</u><br><br>* ↓ <u>endogenous</u> levels with <u>erythropoietin</u><br><br>* normal or ↑ with <u>exogenous</u> <u>androgens</u> [[20]](/library/LP1w2S0)<br><br>* <u>SaO<sub>2</sub></u>: normal<br><br>* Expected plasma volume: normal or ↓ [[21]](/library/pa1Ll20)<br><br><br> | <br>* Use of <u>performance-enhancing drugs</u>, e.g.:<br><br>* <u>Erythropoietin</u><br><br>* <u>Exogenous</u> <u>androgens</u> (e.g., <u>testosterone</u>, <u>anabolic steroids</u>)  [[22]](/library/h6cckW0)<br><br> |  |
| Relative polycythemia |  | <br>* An increase in <u>RBCs</u> in a set blood volume caused by a decreased plasma volume<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>RBC mass</u>: normal or minimally ↑<br><br>* <u>EPO</u>: normal<br><br>* <u>SaO<sub>2</sub></u>: normal<br><br>* Expected plasma volume: ↓<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Severe dehydration</u><br><br>* <u>Gaisböck syndrome</u>  [[23]](/library/0X1e920)<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> An elevated <u>EPO</u> suggests <u>secondary polycythemia</u>. [[17]](/library/kIYm1q)




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

## Treatment

### Approach [[3]](/library/0P1eWS0)[[11]](/library/H_cKpU0)[[15]](/library/R01lf20)[[24]](/library/nPc72c0)




* Consult <u>hematology</u>.

* Assess for acute severe complications, e.g., <u>hyperviscosity syndrome</u>, <u>stroke</u> or <u>pulmonary embolus</u>; if present:

* Manage complications following standard best practice (see relevant articles for details).

* Consider emergency <u>therapeutic phlebotomy</u> or <u>erythrocytapheresis</u> in consultation with <u>hematology</u>.  [[25]](/library/NZc-ba0)[[26]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Assess risk category. [[11]](/library/H_cKpU0)[[27]](/library/c01aU20)

* Low-risk polycythemia vera: no history of <u>thrombosis</u> and ≤ 60 years of age

* High-risk polycythemia vera: history of <u>thrombosis</u> and/or > 60 years of age 11,000–15,000 /mm³ [[11]](/library/H_cKpU0)[[15]](/library/R01lf20)[[28]](/library/5a1iO20)

* All patients

* Regular <u>therapeutic phlebotomy</u> PLUS <u>low-dose aspirin</u>  [[11]](/library/H_cKpU0)

* Manage modifiable cardiovascular <u>risk factors of polycythemia vera</u>.

* Treat associated symptoms, e.g., <u>allopurinol</u> for <u>gout</u>, <u>antihistamines</u> for <u>pruritus</u>.

* Monitor regularly for complications, including transformation to <u>post-PV myelofibrosis</u>, <u>myelodysplastic syndromes</u>, and <u>AML</u>.

* High-risk patients or low-risk patients with persistent symptoms

* Start <u>cytoreductive therapy</u> with <u>hydroxyurea</u>.

* Assess need for anticoagulation.





> [!TIP]
> The management of polycythemia vera focuses on decreasing the risk of <u>thromboembolic events</u>, which are the most common cause of mortality in patients with polycythemia vera. [[3]](/library/0P1eWS0)




> [!TIP]
> <u>Hemopoietic</u> <u>stem cell</u> transplant is not used in the management of polycythemia vera but may be considered in <u>post-PV myelofibrosis</u>. [[13]](/library/FVXgwC)[[24]](/library/nPc72c0)




### Reduction of blood cell counts [[9]](/library/g01F220)[[11]](/library/H_cKpU0)[[15]](/library/R01lf20)[[29]](/library/LPcw2c0)




* Reduction in cell counts decreases hyperviscosity and <u>thromboembolic events</u>.

* Target <u>hematocrit</u>: ≤ 45% [[9]](/library/g01F220)[[15]](/library/R01lf20)[[27]](/library/c01aU20)





#### Regular <u>therapeutic phlebotomy</u>




* Indications: all patients [[3]](/library/0P1eWS0)[[9]](/library/g01F220)[[11]](/library/H_cKpU0)

* Procedure: removal of blood (e.g., 250–500 mL) via <u>venipuncture</u> at scheduled intervals

* Frequency: based on the patient's response to treatment . [[3]](/library/0P1eWS0)





#### <u>Cytoreductive therapy</u> [[3]](/library/0P1eWS0)[[11]](/library/H_cKpU0)[[24]](/library/nPc72c0)[[27]](/library/c01aU20)




* Indications [[3]](/library/0P1eWS0)[[11]](/library/H_cKpU0)[[27]](/library/c01aU20)

* <u>High-risk polycythemia vera</u>

* <u>Low-risk polycythemia vera</u> with any of the following:

* <u>Polycythemia</u> refractory to <u>phlebotomy</u>

* Persistent or progressive symptoms despite <u>phlebotomy</u> and <u>aspirin</u> therapy [[17]](/library/kIYm1q)[[27]](/library/c01aU20)

* First-line: <u>hydroxyurea</u> DOSAGE [[3]](/library/0P1eWS0)[[11]](/library/H_cKpU0)

* Alternatives (e.g., refractory to or unable to tolerate <u>hydroxyurea</u>) [[3]](/library/0P1eWS0)[[11]](/library/H_cKpU0)

* <u>JAK2 inhibitor</u>, e.g., <u>ruxolitinib</u> (in patients with <u>symptomatic splenomegaly</u>)

* <u>Pegylated</u> <u>interferon-alpha</u>

* <u>Busulfan</u> (in older patients)  [[11]](/library/H_cKpU0)[[15]](/library/R01lf20)[[27]](/library/c01aU20)





### Further prevention of <u>thromboembolic events</u> [[11]](/library/H_cKpU0)[[15]](/library/R01lf20)[[24]](/library/nPc72c0)




* All patients: Start <u>antiplatelet drugs</u> (e.g., <u>aspirin</u>  DOSAGE) unless contraindicated.   [[11]](/library/H_cKpU0)[[15]](/library/R01lf20)[[24]](/library/nPc72c0)

* <u>High-risk polycythemia vera</u> in patients with previous <u>VTE</u>: Start <u>anticoagulants</u> (e.g., <u>parenteral anticoagulants</u>, <u>oral anticoagulants</u>).





> [!TIP]
> <u>Smoking cessation</u> is associated with a decreased risk of <u>thrombosis</u>. [[3]](/library/0P1eWS0)




> [!WARNING]
> Patients with extreme <u>thrombocytosis</u> may develop <u>acquired von Willebrand disease</u>. If <u>platelet count</u> is > 1,000,000/Î¼L, perform a <u>ristocetin cofactor assay</u> and consider stopping <u>aspirin</u> if ristocetin <u>cofactor</u> activity is < 20%. [[15]](/library/R01lf20)




### Symptomatic management [[11]](/library/H_cKpU0)[[17]](/library/kIYm1q)




* Symptomatic <u>hyperuricemia</u> (e.g., <u>gouty arthritis</u>): Initiate <u>allopurinol</u>.  [[17]](/library/kIYm1q)

* <u>Pruritus</u>: Treatments include <u>antihistamines</u>, <u>SSRIs</u>, <u>interferon-alpha</u>, and <u>phototherapy</u>. [[11]](/library/H_cKpU0)

* <u>Erythromelalgia</u> [[30]](/library/rb1fE20)

* Avoidance of triggers, e.g., heat exposure

* <u>Aspirin</u> therapy

* Consider <u>adjuvant analgesics</u>, e.g., <u>gabapentin</u>, if symptoms persist despite <u>aspirin</u>.

* <u>Peptic ulcer prophylaxis</u>: <u>PPIs</u> or <u>H<sub>2</sub> receptor blockers</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>JAK2 inhibitors</u> are highly effective at treating <u>symptomatic splenomegaly</u>; <u>splenectomy</u> is now rarely required in patients with <u>polycythemia</u> vera. [[17]](/library/kIYm1q)




> [!WARNING]
> Do not treat <u>iron deficiency</u> in patients with <u>polycythemia</u> vera; maintaining <u>iron deficiency</u> prevents rapid reexpansion of <u>RBC mass</u> after <u>phlebotomy</u>. [[17]](/library/kIYm1q)

---

## Complications

Polycythemia vera is a potentially life-threatening disease because of the numerous complications associated with it.




### <u>Thrombotic</u> complications [[5]](/library/boaH0l)[[31]](/library/aP1QWS0)




* Venous <u>thrombosis</u>

* <u>Renal vein thrombosis</u>

* <u>Mesenteric venous thrombosis</u>

* <u>Portal vein</u> obstruction

* <u>Splenic vein thrombosis</u>

* <u>Deep vein thrombosis</u>

* <u>Pulmonary embolism</u>

* <u>Budd-Chiari syndrome</u>

* Arterial <u>thrombosis</u>

* <u>Stroke</u>

* Peripheral <u>arterial emboli</u>

* <u>Myocardial infarction</u> (<u>MI</u>)

* <u>Splenic infarction</u>





![Hepatic venous obstruction in Budd-Chiari syndrome](media/onv90vlw8nh89raiawatbny6.jpg)

Hepatic venous obstruction in Budd-Chiari syndrome

![Splenomegaly and splenic infarction](media/jsyf35mc95x9x3shl7867sgk.jpg)

Splenomegaly and splenic infarction

![Acute and chronic pulmonary emboli](media/jm0rh9oabemfx8d42gq0zlzh.jpg)

Acute and chronic pulmonary emboli




### Hemorrhagic complications [[5]](/library/boaH0l)




* <u>Petechiae</u>

* <u>Epistaxis</u>

* Bleeding <u>gums</u>





### <u>Gout</u> [[5]](/library/boaH0l)



* High cell turnover → increased <u>uric acid</u>




### Late stages [[5]](/library/boaH0l)




* <u>AML</u>, <u>myelodysplastic syndrome</u> (<u>MDS</u>): Additional genetic mutations may cause polycythemia vera to transition to other hematologic diseases.

* Post-polycythemia vera myelofibrosis: <u>fibrotic</u> transformation of the <u>bone marrow</u>





We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.

---
